Polarized fragmenting jet functions in Inclusive and Exclusive Jet Production

Zhong-Bo Kang Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of California, Los Angeles, California 90095, USA Affiliation: Mani L. Abstract

In this work, we present a complete theoretical framework for analyzing the distribution of polarized hadrons within jets, with and without measuring the transverse momentum relative to the standard jet axis. Using soft-collinear effective theory (SCET), we derive the factorization and provide the theoretical calculation of both semi-inclusive and exclusive fragmenting jet functions (FJFs) under longitudinal and transverse polarization. With the polarized FJFs, one gains access to a variety of new observables that can be used for extracting both collinear and transverse momentum dependent parton distribution functions (PDFs) and fragmentation functions (FFs). As examples, we provide numerical results for the spin asymmetry AT​U,Tcos⁡(ϕS−ϕ^Sh)A_{TU,T}^{\cos(\phi_S - \hat{\phi}_{S_h})} from polarized semi-inclusive hadron-in-jet production in polarized p​ppp collisions at RHIC kinematics, where a transversely polarized quark would lead to the transverse spin of the final-state hadron inside the jet and is thus sensitive to the transversity fragmentation functions. Similarly, another spin asymmetry, AT​U,Lcos⁡(ϕq−ϕS)A_{TU,L}^{\cos(\phi_q - \phi_{S})} from polarized exclusive hadron-in-jet production in polarized e​pep collisions at EIC kinematics would allow us to access the helicity fragmentation functions. These observables demonstrate promising potential in investigating transverse momentum dependent PDFs and FFs and are worthwhile for further measurements.

1 Introduction

Jet substructure, originally developed to exploit the flow of energy within jets of particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to enhance new physics searches [1], has since emerged as a primary tool for studying Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Not only has jet substructure been vastly studied in ongoing experiments at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the LHC [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], but also in future facilities such as the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) [8, 9]. For example, at the LHC, the jet substructure has been successfully used to tag the origin of jets in precision measurements and searches for new physics. At both the RHIC and the LHC, the jet substructure has been an important tool for studying the properties of the hot and dense quark-gluon plasma. On the other hand, at the EIC, as a good proxy of parton-level dynamics, jet allows for a clean factorization between the target and current-fragmentation regions, which is generally difficult in hadron productions [10, 11, 12] in deep inelastic scatterings (DIS).

Most recently, one particular set of jet substructure observables, the distribution of hadrons inside the jet, has received a lot of attention [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Studying hadron distribution inside the jet enables us to pinpoint fragmentation functions of various kinds and to explore the elusive hadronization process. They are complementary to the more standard processes, such as semi-inclusive hadron production in deep inelastic scattering and hadron production in e+​e−e^{+}e^{-} collisions, and allow us to study QCD factorization and to test the universality properties of the associated fragmentation functions in different processes [20]. For example, one can measure the distribution of hadrons inside the jet as a function of the hadron momentum fraction zhz_{h}, where zhz_{h} is the ratio of the transverse momentum of the hadron (ph​Tp_{hT}) to that of the jet (pJ​Tp_{JT}), both relative to the beam axis. Such a zhz_{h} dependence can be used for extracting the zhz_{h}-dependence of the collinear fragmentation functions (FFs) [21, 22]. On the other hand, if one measures both zhz_{h} and the transverse momentum 𝒋⊥\bm{j}_{\bot} distribution of the hadrons with respect to the jet axis, one would be able to study the transverse momentum-dependent fragmentation functions (TMD FFs) [23].

The theoretical object which describes the momentum distribution of hadrons inside a fully reconstructed jet is called fragmenting jet functions (FJFs). For the zhz_{h}-dependence while integrating over the hadron’s transverse momentum with respect to the jet axis, we would have collinear FJFs, which can be matched onto the standard collinear FFs. These collinear FJFs have been studied in the so-called semi-inclusive jet production, as well as the exclusive jet production. For semi-inclusive jet production, one measures the signal jet while completely inclusive on other particles in the final state, see the studies in e.g., [24, 25, 21, 26, 27, 28, 29]. On the other hand, in the context being discussed, “exclusive” jet production refers to situations where a fixed number of jets are produced in the final state but one vetoes additional jets. For example, in the back-to-back electron-jet production in electron-proton collisions, our factorization would depend on the exclusive FJFs, where we have an electron and a single signal jet in the final state. See the studies along this line [30, 31, 32, 33, 34]. On the other hand, measuring both zhz_{h} and 𝒋⊥\bm{j}_{\bot} distribution of the hadrons with respect to the standard jet axis would give us the transverse momentum dependent fragmenting jet functions (TMD FJFs). There are close relationships [35, 23, 36, 37, 27] between these TMD FJFs and the standard TMD FFs [38, 39, 40]. More recently, studies have been advanced to the polarized sector, including the polarization of both the parton initiating the jet and the hadron produced within the jet [34, 41, 42, 43]. For a recent study exploring dihadron fragmentation functions (or two hadrons) inside the jet, see [44, 45]. For the TMD study of the hadron with respect to the Winner-Take-All jet axis, see [46, 37, 47, 48]. As for the TMD study inside the groomed jet, see [36, 49, 50]. More recently, exploring the connections between TMD physics and the energy-energy correlators has seen a lot of progress [51, 52, 53].

For the polarized collinear FJFs and TMD FJFs, we have performed studies in previous publications, mainly in [34, 41] for semi-inclusive and exclusive jet productions. Even though we provided theoretical formalism and illustrated some phenomenological studies there, for the computations of FJFs, only partial results were available in those previous publications, but not the complete full results. This is the goal of our current paper. We will perform all the relevant computations and give all associated matching coefficients that allow us to connect these FJFs to the standard FFs. In doing so, we also update our formalism using the more recent approach outlined in the TMD Handbook [13]. We provide additional phenomenological studies at the RHIC and the future EIC.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we establish the theoretical foundation for collinear FJFs, elucidate a number of correlations between the polarization of the hadrons and fragmenting partons, and illuminate their physical significance and connections to standard fragmentation functions. In Section 3, we introduce the semi-inclusive and exclusive TMD FJFs. We discuss their factorization and evolution properties, as well as their relations to the standard TMD FFs. In Section 4, we employ this framework to predict the spin asymmetry AT​U,Tcos⁡(ϕS−ϕ^Sh)A_{TU,T}^{\cos(\phi_S - \hat{\phi}_{S_h})} for the semi-inclusive production of transversely polarized Λ\Lambda baryons inside jet in transversely polarized p​ppp collisions at RHIC kinematics, and AT​U,Lcos⁡(ϕq−ϕS)A_{TU,L}^{\cos(\phi_q - \phi_{S})} for the exclusive production of longitudinally polarized Λ/Λ¯\Lambda/\overline{\Lambda} inside jet in polarized e​pep collisions at EIC kinematics. Finally, we provide a summary of our findings in Section 5. We collect a few additional details in the Appendix.

2 The collinear fragmenting jet functions (FJFs)

In this section, we introduce the definition of the semi-inclusive and exclusive fragmenting jet functions (FJFs) in soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) [54, 55, 56, 57, 58] with both unpolarized and polarized fragmenting hadron. Such FJFs are used to describe the longitudinal momentum fraction distribution of hadrons within jets. We first provide the operator definitions of FJFs, then perform the calculation to NLO, and lastly derive and solve the RG evolution equations.

2.1 Collinear FJFs in semi-inclusive jet productions

We can construct the semi-inclusive fragmenting quark and gluon jet functions using the corresponding gauge invariant quark and gluon fields in SCET which are given by:

χn=Wn†​ξn,ℬn⟂μ=1g​[Wn†​i​Dn⟂μ​Wn],\chi_{n}=W_{n}^{\dagger}\xi_{n}\,,\quad\mathcal{B}_{n\perp}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{g}\bqty{W_n^{\dagger} i D_{n \perp}^{\mu} W_n}\,, (1)

where the subscript nn indicates that the field is along the nn-collinear direction, and nμ=(1,0,0,1)n^{\mu}=\pqty{1, 0, 0, 1} is the light-cone vector whose spatial component is aligned with the jet axis. In Eq. 1, the covariant derivative is i​Dn⟂μ=𝒫n⟂μ+g​An⟂μiD_{n\perp}^{\mu}=\mathcal{P}_{n\perp}^{\mu}+gA_{n\perp}^{\mu}, where 𝒫μ\mathcal{P}^{\mu} is the label momentum operator. Moreover, WnW_{n} is the Wilson line of collinear gluons:

Wn​(x)=∑permsexp(−g1n¯⋅𝒫n¯⋅An(x)).W_{n}\pqty{x}=\sum_{\textrm{perms}}\exp(-g \frac{1}{\overline{n} \cdot\mathcal{P}} \overline{n} \cdot A_n \pqty{x})\,. (2)

It is also useful to define the conjugate light-cone vector n¯μ=(1,0,0,−1)\overline{n}^{\mu}=(1,0,0,-1), such that n2=n¯2=0n^{2}=\overline{n}^{2}=0 and n⋅n¯=2n\cdot\overline{n}=2. Thus, any four-vector pμp^{\mu} can be decomposed as pμ=[p+,p−,𝒑⟂]p^{\mu}=\bqty{p^+, p^-, \boldsymbol{p}_{\perp}}11 1 We use square bracket for vectors written in light cone coordinates., where p+=n⋅pp^{+}=n\cdot p and p−=n¯⋅pp^{-}=\overline{n}\cdot p, namely:

pμ=p−​nμ2+p+​n¯μ2+p⟂μ.p^{\mu}=p^{-}\frac{n^{\mu}}{2}+p^{+}\frac{\overline{n}^{\mu}}{2}+p_{\perp}^{\mu}\,. (3)

For a hadron in the reference frame where it has no transverse momentum and moves along the +z+z-direction, it will have a large ph−p_{h}^{-} component and a small ph+p_{h}^{+} component, i.e., ph+≪ph−p_{h}^{+}\ll p_{h}^{-}. Thus the momentum php_{h} and spin ShS_{h} of the hadron inside the jet can be parameterized as:

ph=[Mh2ph−,ph−,𝟎],Sh=[−λh​Mhph−,λh​ph−Mh,𝑺h⟂].\displaystyle p_{h}=\bqty{\frac{M_h^2}{p_h^-}, p_h^-, \boldsymbol{0}}\,,\quad S_{h}=\bqty{- \lambda_h \frac{M_h}{p_h^-}, \lambda_h \frac{p_h^-}{M_h}, \boldsymbol{S}_{h\perp}}\,. (4)

Here λh\lambda_{h} is the helicity of the hadron with mass MhM_{h}, and 𝑺h⟂\bm{S}_{h\perp} is the transverse polarization of the hadron inside the jet.

2.1.1 NLO calculation

Although the semi-inclusive FJFs 𝒢ih​(z,zh,pT​R,μ)\mathcal{G}_{i}^{h}\pqty{z, z_h, p_TR, \mu} are not perturbatively calculable, they can be matched onto the standard collinear fragmentation functions as long as pT​R≫ΛQCDp_{T}R\gg\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} [21]. The matching coefficients can be computed by replacing the hadron hh by a parton jj and then computing 𝒢ij​(z,zh,pT​R,μ)\mathcal{G}_{i}^{j}\pqty{z, z_h, p_TR, \mu} perturbatively. Prior to describing the process of computing the semi-inclusive FJFs, it is important to emphasize that the outcomes are influenced by the choice of jet algorithms. To streamline our explanation, however, we solely concentrate on the anti-kTk_{T} algorithm [62] in this study.

We will now compute the bare partonic semi-inclusive FJFs 𝒢ij​(z,zh,pT​R)\mathcal{G}_{i}^{j}\pqty{z, z_h, p_TR} in order to determine the UV counter terms. At the leading order (LO), one has a single parton. It is this parton ii that forms the jet as well as presenting the parton jj inside the jet. Thus we have z=1z=1 and zh=1z_{h}=1 at LO and bare polarized semi-inclusive FJFs are given by:

Δ(T)​𝒢ij,(0)​(z,zh,pT​R)=δi​j​δ​(1−z)​δ​(1−zh).\Delta_{(T)}\mathcal{G}_{i}^{j,(0)}(z,z_{h},p_{T}R)=\delta_{ij}\delta(1-z)\delta(1-z_{h})\,. (11)

Here and throughout the rest of the paper, we use the symbol Δ(T)\Delta_{(T)} to collectively represent both the longitudinally (Δ\Delta) and transversely (TT) polarized cases.

At the next-to-leading order (NLO), we have to consider the 1→21\to 2 splitting process in the real emission diagrams as shown in , as well as virtual diagrams. In dimensional regularization, since virtual diagrams become scaleless integrals and vanish, we thus only consider the real diagrams. Following the discussion in [21], we consider the cases of both partons in the jet and only one parton in the jet as shown in . They are given by the same integrals over the transverse momentum q⊥q_{\bot} of the parton jj, but are constrained by different Heaviside functions. Working in pure dimensional regularization with d=4−2​ϵd=4-2\epsilon dimensions, we have:

Δ(T)​𝒢ij,(1)​(z,zh,ωJ)\displaystyle\Delta_{(T)}\mathcal{G}_{i}^{j,(1)}(z,z_{h},\omega_{J}) =αs2​π​(eγE​μ2)ϵΓ⁡(1−ϵ)​(δ⁡(1−z)​Δ(T)​P^j​i​(zh,ϵ)​∫dq⟂2(q⟂2)1+ϵ​Θbothanti-​kTCLOSE\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2\pi}\frac{(e^{\gamma_{E}}\mu^{2})^{\epsilon}}{\Gamma(1-\epsilon)}\bigg(\delta(1-z)\Delta_{(T)}\hat{P}_{ji}(z_{h},\epsilon)\int\frac{\differential{q_{\perp}^2}}{(q_{\perp}^{2})^{1+\epsilon}}\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{\mathrm{both}}
+δ(1−zh)Δ(T)P^j​i(z,ϵ)∫dq⟂2(q⟂2)1+ϵΘjanti-​kT),\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad+\delta(1-z_{h})\Delta_{(T)}\hat{P}_{ji}(z,\epsilon)\int\frac{\differential{q_{\perp}^2}}{(q_{\perp}^{2})^{1+\epsilon}}\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{j}\bigg)\,, (12)

where the Θbothanti-​kT\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{\mathrm{both}} and Θjanti-​kT\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{j} are the jet algorithm constraints with both partons in jet (A) and only one parton in jet (B, C), respectively, and the superscript “anti-kTk_{T}” indicates that anti-kTk_{T} algorithm is used. The form of Θbothanti-​kT\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{\mathrm{both}} and Θjanti-​kT\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{j} are given by the Heaviside functions [64, 21, 65]:

Θbothanti-​kT\displaystyle\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{\textrm{both}} =θ​(zh​(1−zh)​ωJ​tan⁡(ℛ2)−q⟂),\displaystyle=\theta\pqty{z_h (1 - z_h) \omega_J \tan{\frac{\mathcal{R}}{2}} - q_{\perp}}\,, (13)
Θjanti-​kT\displaystyle\Theta^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}_{j} =θ​(q⟂−(1−z)​ωJ​tan⁡ℛ2),\displaystyle=\theta\pqty{q_{\perp} - (1 - z) \omega_J \tan\frac{\mathcal{R}}{2}}\,, (14)

where ℛ\mathcal{R} is the angular separation between three vector momenta inside the jet [64]. This is to be compared with the jet radius RR in the hadron collider that specifies the separation in pseudo-rapidity and azimuthal angle as in (Δ​η)2+(Δ​ϕ)2\sqrt{(\Delta\eta)^{2}+(\Delta\phi)^{2}}. For jets with a small jet radius R≪1R\ll 1, we have

ℛ=Rcosh⁡(η),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}=\frac{R}{\cosh(\eta)}\,, (15)

where η\eta is the jet pseudo-rapidity. Note that

ωJ​tan⁡ℛ2≈2​EJ​ℛ2=pT​cosh⁡(η)​Rcosh⁡(η)=pT​R,\displaystyle\omega_{J}\tan\frac{\mathcal{R}}{2}\approx 2E_{J}\,\frac{\mathcal{R}}{2}=p_{T}\cosh(\eta)\frac{R}{\cosh(\eta)}=p_{T}R\,, (16)

and we will thus include the argument pT​Rp_{T}R in the FJFs.

The longitudinally polarized functions Δ​P^j​i​(z,ϵ)\Delta\hat{P}_{ji}(z,\epsilon) in 12 are given in [66]:

Δ​P^q​q​(z,ϵ)\displaystyle\Delta\hat{P}_{qq}(z,\epsilon) =CF​[1+z21−z−ϵ⁡(1−z)],\displaystyle=C_{F}\bqty{\frac{1 + z^2}{1 - z} - \epsilon(1 - z)}\,, (17)
Δ​P^g​q​(z,ϵ)\displaystyle\Delta\hat{P}_{gq}(z,\epsilon) =CF​[2−z+2​ϵ​(1−z)],\displaystyle=C_{F}\bqty{2 - z + 2 \epsilon(1 - z)}\,, (18)
Δ​P^q​g​(z,ϵ)\displaystyle\Delta\hat{P}_{qg}(z,\epsilon) =TF​[2​z−1−2​ϵ​(1−z)],\displaystyle=T_{F}\bqty{2 z - 1 - 2 \epsilon(1 - z)}\,, (19)
Δ​P^g​g​(z,ϵ)\displaystyle\Delta\hat{P}_{gg}(z,\epsilon) =2​CA​[11−z−2​z+1+2​ϵ​(1−z)].\displaystyle=2C_{A}\bqty{\frac{1}{1 - z} - 2 z + 1 + 2 \epsilon(1 - z)}\,. (20)

The transversely polarized splitting functions ΔT​P^j​i​(z,ϵ)\Delta_{T}\hat{P}_{ji}(z,\epsilon) only exist for ΔT​P^q​q\Delta_{T}\hat{P}_{qq} because there is no gluon transversity fragmentation function for spin-1/2 hadron as we mentioned above. We have the following expression for ΔT​P^q​q​(z,ϵ)\Delta_{T}\hat{P}_{qq}(z,\epsilon) [67]

ΔT​P^q​q​(z,ϵ)=CF​[2​z1−z].\Delta_{T}\hat{P}_{qq}(z,\epsilon)=C_{F}\left[\frac{2z}{1-z}\right]\,. (21)

By inserting the Θ\Theta functions for anti-kTk_{T} algorithm and carrying out the integration in 12, we obtain the bare results22 2 More details on the q⟂q_{\perp} integral and relevant expansions as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 can be found in Appendix A. for longitudinally polarized semi-inclusive FJFs Δ​𝒢i,barej​(z,zh,pT​R)\Delta\mathcal{G}^{j}_{i,\mathrm{bare}}(z,z_{h},p_{T}R) with i,j∈{q,g}i,j\in\Bqty{q, g}:

Δ​𝒢q,bareq\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{G}^{q}_{q,\mathrm{bare}} (z,zh,pT​R)=δ⁡(1−z)​δ​(1−zh)\displaystyle(z,z_{h},p_{T}R)=\delta(1-z)\delta(1-z_{h})

+δ⁡(1−z)​αs2​π​[2​Δ​Pq​g​(zh)​ln⁡(zh​(1−zh))+2​TF​(1−zh)]\displaystyle+\delta(1-z)\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2\pi}\bigg[2\Delta P_{qg}(z_{h})\ln(z_h (1-z_h))+2T_{F}(1-z_{h})\bigg]

ΔT​𝒢q,bareq\displaystyle\Delta_{T}\mathcal{G}^{q}_{q,\mathrm{bare}} (z,zh,pT​R)=δ⁡(1−z)​δ​(1−zh)\displaystyle(z,z_{h},p_{T}R)=\delta(1-z)\delta(1-z_{h})

2.1.2 Renormalization and matching onto collinear FFs

In this section, we will renormalize the bare semi-inclusive FJFs obtained in the previous section, and then match the results to the standard collinear FFs. In doing so, it is important to point out that the 1/ϵ1/\epsilon poles with a factor of Δ(T)​Pi​j​(zh)​δ​(1−z)\Delta_{\pqty{T}}P_{ij}\pqty{z_h}\delta\pqty{1 - z} in Eqs. 22, 23, 24, 25 and 27 are the infrared (IR) poles, that would be matched onto the standard longitudinally (transversely) polarized collinear FFs. On the other hand, the poles with a factor of Δ(T)​Pi​j​(z)​δ​(1−zh)\Delta_{\pqty{T}}P_{ij}\pqty{z}\delta\pqty{1 - z_h} are the ultraviolet (UV) poles which will be taken care of by renormalization. Since the UV poles do not involve the variable zhz_{h}, we should expect that zhz_{h} is merely a parameter in renormalization. This is exactly the same as the unpolarized situation studied in [21]. With this in mind, the relationship between the bare and renormalized semi-inclusive FJFs is given by

Δ(T)​𝒢i,barej​(z,zh,pT​R)=∑k∫z1dz′z′​Δ(T)​Zi​k​(zz′,μ)​Δ(T)​𝒢kj​(z′,zh,pT​R,μ),\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{i,\mathrm{bare}}^{j}\pqty{z, z_h, p_T R}=\sum_{k}\int_{z}^{1}\frac{\differential{z'}}{z^{\prime}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}Z_{ik}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}, \mu}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{k}^{j}\pqty{z', z_h, p_T R, \mu}\,, (34)

where Δ(T)​Zi​k​(zz′,μ)\Delta_{\pqty{T}}Z_{ik}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}, \mu} is the renormalization matrix and Δ(T)​𝒢kj​(z′,zh,pT​R,μ)\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{k}^{j}\pqty{z', z_h, p_T R, \mu} are the renormalized semi-inclusive FJFs. For the aforementioned reason, the convolution only involves the variable zz. The renormalized semi-inclusive FJFs satisfy the following RG evolution equations:

μ​ddμ​Δ(T)​𝒢ij​(z,zh,pT​R,μ)=∑k∫z1dz′z′​Δ(T)​γi​k𝒢​(zz′,μ)​Δ(T)​𝒢kj​(z′,zh,pT​R,μ),\mu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\mu}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{i}^{j}\pqty{z, z_h, p_TR, \mu}=\sum_{k}\int_{z}^{1}\frac{\differential{z'}}{z^{\prime}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\gamma_{ik}^{\mathcal{G}}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}, \mu}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{k}^{j}\pqty{z', z_h, p_T R, \mu}\,, (35)

with the anomalous dimension matrix given by:

Δ(T)γi​k𝒢(zz′,μ)=−∑k∫z1dz′z′(Δ(T)​Z)i​l−1(zz′,μ)μddμΔ(T)Zl​k(z′,μ),\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\gamma_{ik}^{\mathcal{G}}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}, \mu}=-\sum_{k}\int_{z}^{1}\frac{\differential{z'}}{z^{\prime}}\pqty{\Delta_{\pqty{T}} Z}_{il}^{-1}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}, \mu}\mu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\mu}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}Z_{lk}\pqty{z', \mu}\,, (36)

and (Δ(T)​Z)i​l−1\pqty{\Delta_{\pqty{T}} Z}_{il}^{-1} is the inverse of the renormalization matrix that is defined such that:

∑k∫z1dz′z′​(Δ(T)​Z)i​l−1​(zz′,μ)​Δ(T)​Zl​j​(z′,μ)=δi​j​δ​(1−z).\sum_{k}\int_{z}^{1}\frac{\differential{z'}}{z^{\prime}}\pqty{\Delta_{\pqty{T}} Z}_{il}^{-1}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}, \mu}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}Z_{lj}\pqty{z', \mu}=\delta_{ij}\delta\pqty{1 - z}\,. (37)

Up to 𝒪⁡(αs)\order{\alpha_s}, the renormalization matrix is

Δ(T)​Zi​j​(z,μ)=δi​j​δ​(1−z)+αs​(μ)2​π​1ϵ​Δ(T)​Pj​i​(z),\Delta_{\pqty{T}}Z_{ij}\pqty{z, \mu}=\delta_{ij}\delta\pqty{1 - z}+\frac{\alpha_{s}\pqty{\mu}}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}P_{ji}\pqty{z}\,, (38)

and therefore the anomalous dimension matrix is given by:

Δ(T)​γi​j𝒢​(z,μ)=αs​(μ)π​Δ(T)​Pj​i​(z).\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\gamma_{ij}^{\mathcal{G}}\pqty{z, \mu}=\frac{\alpha_{s}\pqty{\mu}}{\pi}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}P_{ji}\pqty{z}\,. (39)

We therefore observe that the evolution of the renormalized polarized semi-inclusive FJFs conforms to the time-like DGLAP equation for collinear polarized FFs [68]:

μ​ddμ​Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(z,zh,pT​R,μ)=αs​(μ)π​∑k∫z1dz′z′​Δ(T)​Pj​i​(zz′)​Δ(T)​𝒢jh​(z′,zh,pT​R,μ),\mu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\mu}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{i}^{h}\pqty{z, z_h, p_TR, \mu}=\frac{\alpha_{s}\pqty{\mu}}{\pi}\sum_{k}\int_{z}^{1}\frac{\differential{z'}}{z^{\prime}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}P_{ji}\pqty{\frac{z}{z'}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{j}^{h}\pqty{z', z_h, p_TR, \mu}\,, (40)

where the leading order splitting kernels are given in Eqs. 28, 29, 30, 31 and 32. Notice that the hadronic FJFs have been reinstated since the hadronic and partonic FJFs would contain the same UV counter terms and thus follow the same RG evolution equations. As we mentioned in the previous section that the natural scale for the collinear FJFs is given by μ𝒢=pT​R\mu_{\mathscr{G}}=p_{T}R, thus one would use the above renormalization group equations to evolve these FJFs from their natural scale pT​Rp_{T}R to the hard scale pTp_{T} for the jet production. The effect of this would be to resum the logarithms of the jet radius RR for narrow jets with R≪1R\ll 1. Analogous behaviors were observed in the context of the semi-inclusive unpolarized FJFs in [21].

With the UV poles eliminated by renormalization, we can proceed to dealing with the IR poles, which can be addressed by matching onto the collinear polarized FFs. Such matching can be done at a scale μ≫ΛQCD\mu\gg\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} as follows:

Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(z,zh,pT​R,μ)=∑j∫zh1dzh′zh′​Δ(T)​𝒥i​j​(z,zh′,pT​R,μ)​Δ(T)​Dh/j​(zhzh′,μ),\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{G}_{i}^{h}\pqty{z, z_h, p_TR, \mu}=\sum_{j}\int_{z_{h}}^{1}\frac{\differential{z_h'}}{z_{h}^{\prime}}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{J}_{ij}\pqty{z, z_h', p_TR, \mu}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}D_{h/j}\pqty{\frac{z_h}{z_h'}, \mu}\,, (41)

where again, the hadronic semi-inclusive FJFs and collinear FFs are reinstated. Here, Δ(T)​Dh/j​(zh,μ)\Delta_{(T)}D_{h/j}(z_{h},\mu) is the collinear fragmentation function characterizing a parton jj fragmenting into a hadron hh. Specifically, Δ​Dh/j\Delta D_{h/j} (ΔT​Dh/j\Delta_{T}D_{h/j}) is the helicity (transversity) fragmentation function describing a longitudinally (transversely) polarized parton fragmenting into a longitudinally (transversely) polarized hadron. And the matching relation above holds, with a power correction of order 𝒪⁡(ΛQCD2/(OPENpT​R)2))\order{\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}^2 / \pqty{p_TR)^2}} [31, 33, 21]. In this case, however, different from the renormalization procedure, zhz_{h} is being convoluted and zz is merely a parameter. This process is similar to the approach used for unpolarized FJFs described in [21], except that instead of the unpolarized FFs, collinear polarized FFs are used in this case. The perturbative results at the parton level for the polarized collinear FFs are given by:

Δ(T)​Dj/i​(zh,μ)=δi​j​δ​(1−zh)+αs2​π​Δ(T)​Pj​i​(zh)​(−1ϵ).\Delta_{\pqty{T}}D_{j/i}\pqty{z_h, \mu}=\delta_{ij}\delta\pqty{1-z_h}+\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2\pi}\Delta_{\pqty{T}}P_{ji}\pqty{z_h}\pqty{-\frac{1}{\epsilon}}\,. (42)

Finally, the matching coefficients Δ(T)​𝒥i​j\Delta_{\pqty{T}}\mathcal{J}_{ij} for anti-kTk_{T} jet algorithm are as follows

Δ​𝒥q​q​(z,zh,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{J}_{qq}(z,z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) =δ(1−z)δ(1−zh)+αs2​π{L[ΔPq​q(z)δ(1−zh)−ΔPq​q(zh)δ(1−z)]\displaystyle=\delta(1-z)\delta(1-z_{h})+\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2\pi}\bigg\{L\bigg[\Delta P_{qq}(z)\delta(1-z_{h})-\Delta P_{qq}(z_{h})\delta(1-z)\bigg]
+δ⁡(1−z)​[2​CF​(1+zh2)​(ln⁡(1−zh)1−zh)++CF​(1−zh)+Δ​ℐq​qanti-​kT​(zh)]\displaystyle\quad+\delta(1-z)\bqty{2 C_F (1+z_h^2) \pqty{\frac{\ln(1-z_h)}{1-z_h}}_+ + C_F (1-z_h) + \Delta\mathcal{I}_{qq}^{\text{anti-}k_T}(z_h)}
−δ(1−zh)[2​CF​(1+z2)​(ln⁡(1−z)1−z)++CF​(1−z)]},\displaystyle\quad-\delta(1-z_{h})\bqty{2 C_F (1+z^2) \pqty{\frac{\ln(1-z)}{1-z}}_+ + C_F (1-z)}\bigg\}\,, (43)

+δ⁡(1−z)​[2​Δ​Pq​g​(zh)​ln⁡(1−zh)+2​TF​(1−zh)+Δ​ℐq​ganti-​kT​(zh)]\displaystyle\quad+\delta(1-z)\bigg[2\Delta P_{qg}(z_{h})\ln(1-z_h)+2T_{F}(1-z_{h})+\Delta\mathcal{I}_{qg}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h})\bigg]

−δ(1−zh)[4​CF​z​(ln⁡(1−z)1−z)+]},\displaystyle\quad-\delta(1-z_{h})\bqty{4 C_F z \pqty{\frac{\ln(1-z)}{1-z}}_+}\bigg\}\,, (47)

The matching coefficient functions Δ​𝒥i​j\Delta\mathcal{J}_{ij} for the longitudinally polarized case have been given in the previous publication [34] with a different notation 𝒥i​jL\mathcal{J}^{L}_{ij}. Here, we provide the detailed steps of how such matching coefficients are derived. At the same time, the matching coefficient for the transversely polarized case ΔT​𝒥q​q\Delta_{T}\mathcal{J}_{qq} is presented here for the first time.

2.2 Collinear FJFs in exclusive jet productions

Exclusive jet production, such as back-to-back dijet production in proton-proton collisions [69, 70] or back-to-back electron-jet production in electron-proton collisions [71], can provide valuable insight into the understanding of the fundamental dynamics of hadron structure and interactions. However, in such situations, typically the radiation outside the jet is restricted. For example, in back-to-back dijet production, one usually restricts the transverse momentum imbalance qTq_{T} to be much smaller than the average transverse momentum of the jets. In this case, the hard/collinear gluon emission outside the jet would move the imbalance qTq_{T} away from the back-to-back region. Because of that, the collinear radiation can only happen inside the jet. Consequently, for jet function calculations in exclusive jet production, we only have to consider A while B and C would not contribute. We refer to the corresponding FJFs as exclusive FJFs below, which are key ingredients in the factorization formalism for these processes. They describe the probability distribution for a parton in the jet to fragment into a hadron with a given collinear momentum fraction in exclusive jet production.

The perturbative computations for exclusive FJFs Δ(T)​𝒢ij​(zh,pT​R,μ)\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{j}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) are identical to those for the semi-inclusive FJFs, except that we keep only the contributions from A. Since both partons are always inside the jet, we always have z=1z=1, i.e., the jet carries all the energy of the parton that initiates the jet in this case. Because of this, we no longer keep the variable zz in the FJFs and thus the exclusive FJFs only depend on zhz_{h}. The RG equations for exclusive FJFs can also be derived in the same manner as above, and we find that they satisfy the following equation

μ​ddμ​Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(zh,pT​R,μ)=γ𝒢i​(μ)​Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(zh,pT​R,μ),\mu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\mu}}\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{h}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu)=\gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{i}(\mu)\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{h}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu)\,, (49)

where the index ii is not summed over, and the anomalous dimensions γ𝒢i​(μ)\gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{i}(\mu) with i=qi=q, gg at this order are given by:

γ𝒢q​(μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{q}(\mu) =αs​(μ)π​(CF​L+32​CF),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}(\mu)}{\pi}\pqty{C_F L + \frac{3}{2}C_F}\,, (50)
γ𝒢g​(μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{g}(\mu) =αs​(μ)π​(CA​L+β02).\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}(\mu)}{\pi}\pqty{C_A L + \frac{\beta_0}{2}}\,. (51)

A few comments are in order. First of all, it is important to emphasize that the RG equation for exclusive FJFs is a multiplicative renormalization, instead of a convolution over zz as in the semi-inclusive FJFs given in the previous section. Secondly, the anomalous dimension γ𝒢i​(μ)\gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^{i}(\mu) is the same as that of the exclusive jet functions in [64] and exclusive unpolarized FJFs [27, 33, 72]. Since in the factorization formalism, one simply replaces the exclusive jet function with the exclusive FJFs, thus they should have the same anomalous dimensions simply because of the RG consistency. At the same time, we find that the UV divergent terms are all proportional to δ⁡(1−zh)\delta(1-z_{h}) where the radiated gluon becomes soft, and thus the result should be independent of the polarization of the partons. This explains the anomalous dimensions for both longitudinally and transversely polarized FJFs are the same as the unpolarized FJFs. The solution to the RG equation for the exclusive FJFs is then:

Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(zh,pT​R,μ)=Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(zh,pT​R,μ𝒢)​exp⁡[∫μ𝒢μdμ′μ′​γ𝒢i​(μ′)],\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{h}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu)=\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{h}\pqty{z_h, p_TR, \mu_{\mathscr{G}}}\exp\bqty{\int_{\mu_{\mathscr{G}}}^\mu\frac{\dd{\mu^{\prime}}}{\mu^{\prime}} \gamma_{\mathscr{G}}^i\pqty{\mu^{\prime}}}\,, (52)

where the scale μ𝒢\mu_{\mathscr{G}} is the characteristic scale that eliminates the large logarithms in the fixed-order perturbative calculations. The logarithm LL indicates that the natural scale for the exclusive FJFs is also given by μ𝒢=pT​R\mu_{\mathscr{G}}=p_{T}R, the same as for the semi-inclusive FJFs. One would thus evolve the FJFs from the natural scale μ𝒢∼pT​R\mu_{\mathscr{G}}\sim p_{T}R to the hard scale of the process μ∼pT\mu\sim p_{T} and effectively resum the logarithm of jet radius, ln⁡R\ln R.

Finishing the discussion on the RG equation for the exclusive FJFs, let us now turn to their matching to the standard collinear FFs. Similar to the semi-inclusive FJFs, the exclusive fragmenting jet functions Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(zh,pT​R,μ)\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{h}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) are also closely related to the fragmentation functions Δ(T)​Dh/j\Delta_{(T)}D_{h/j} and in this work we label the corresponding matching coefficients as Δ(T)​𝒥i​j\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{J}_{ij}. Following [31, 72, 33, 27], one has the following expansion for exclusive FJFs:

Δ(T)​𝒢ih​(zh,pT​R,μ)=∑j∫zh1dzh′zh′​Δ(T)​𝒥i​j​(zh′,pT​R,μ)​Δ(T)​Dh/j​(zhzh′,μ).\displaystyle\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{G}_{i}^{h}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu)=\sum_{j}\int_{z_{h}}^{1}\frac{\differential{z'_h}}{z^{\prime}_{h}}\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{J}_{ij}(z^{\prime}_{h},p_{T}R,\mu)\Delta_{(T)}D_{h/j}\pqty{\frac{z_h}{z'_h}, \mu}\,. (53)

Again this equation is valid up to power corrections of order 𝒪⁡(ΛQCD2/(OPENpT​R)2))\order{\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}^2 / \pqty{p_TR)^2}} for light hadrons. For heavy meson fragmenting jet functions, ΛQCD\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} should be replaced by the heavy quark mass mQm_{Q} in the above equation [33, 73]. We provide the NLO results of matching coefficients Δ(T)​𝒥i​j\Delta_{(T)}\mathscr{J}_{ij}, which depend on the jet algorithm. The results for unpolarized FJFs with cone algorithm were given in [74], while those for anti-kTk_{T} jets were first written down in [72]. While the results for the unpolarized FJFs are available in the literature, the coefficients for the polarized FJFs are given for the first time in our current paper. We provide the detailed derivations of exclusive FJFs with polarizations for anti-kTk_{T} jets in Appendix B. Here we only list the final results:

Δ​𝒥q​q​(zh,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\Delta\mathscr{J}_{qq}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) =δ(1−zh)+αs​CF2​π[δ(1−zh)(L22−π212)−ΔPq​q(zh)L\displaystyle=\delta(1-z_{h})+\frac{\alpha_{s}C_{F}}{2\pi}\bigg[\delta(1-z_{h})\pqty{\frac{L^2}{2} - \frac{\pi^2}{12}}-\Delta P_{qq}(z_{h})L
+1−zh+Δℐ^q​qanti-​kT(zh)],\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad+1-z_{h}+\Delta\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{qq}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h})\bigg]\,, (54)
Δ​𝒥q​g​(zh,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\Delta\mathscr{J}_{qg}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) =αs​CF2​π​[−Δ​Pg​q​(zh)​L−2​(1−zh)+Δ​ℐ^q​ganti-​kT​(zh)],\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}C_{F}}{2\pi}\bigg[-\Delta P_{gq}(z_{h})L-2(1-z_{h})+\Delta\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{qg}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h})\bigg]\,, (55)
Δ​𝒥g​q​(zh,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\Delta\mathscr{J}_{gq}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) =αs​TF2​π​[−Δ​Pq​g​(zh)​L+2​(1−zh)+Δ​ℐ^g​qanti-​kT​(zh)],\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}T_{F}}{2\pi}\bigg[-\Delta P_{qg}(z_{h})L+2(1-z_{h})+\Delta\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{gq}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h})\bigg]\,, (56)

−4(1−zh)+Δℐ^g​ganti-​kT(zh)],\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad-4(1-z_{h})+\Delta\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{gg}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h})\bigg]\,, (57)
ΔT​𝒥q​q​(zh,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\Delta_{T}\mathscr{J}_{qq}(z_{h},p_{T}R,\mu) =δ(1−zh)+αs​CF2​π[δ(1−zh)(L22−π212)\displaystyle=\delta(1-z_{h})+\frac{\alpha_{s}C_{F}}{2\pi}\bigg[\delta(1-z_{h})\pqty{\frac{L^2}{2} - \frac{\pi^2}{12}}
−ΔTPq​q(zh)L+ΔTℐ^qanti-​kT(zh)],\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad-\Delta_{T}P_{qq}(z_{h})L+\Delta_{T}\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{q}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h})\bigg]\,, (58)

where for anti-kTk_{T} jets, the jet-algorithm dependent pieces, Δ(T)​ℐ^i​janti-​kT​(zh)\Delta_{(T)}\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{ij}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}(z_{h}), are given by

Δ​ℐ^q​qanti-​kT​(zh)\displaystyle\Delta\hat{\mathscr{I}}_{qq}^{\text{anti-}k_{T}}\pqty{z_h} =2​Δ​Pq​q​(zh)​ln⁡(zh)+2​(1+zh2)​(ln⁡(1−zh)1−zh)+,\displaystyle=2\Delta P_{qq}(z_{h})\ln(z_h)+2\pqty{1+z_h^2}\pqty{\frac{\ln(1-z_h)}{1-z_h}}_{+}\,, (59)

3 The transverse momentum dependent FJFs (TMD FJFs)

In this section, we study TMD FJFs in both the semi-inclusive jet production and the exclusive jet production, including polarizations of the initiating parton and the final observed hadron inside the jet. They are termed as polarized TMD FJFs [34]. Some partial results are available in the previous publications [34, 41], but never the complete results. For example, the hard matching functions for both longitudinally and transversely polarized cases are presented for the first time. Below, we provide the complete results for all the relevant polarized semi-inclusive and exclusive TMD FJFs. The operator definitions of these functions in SCET are presented, followed by their factorization formalism, which involves hard functions, soft functions, and TMD FFs.

The kinematics is set up as in Fig. 3, a hadron hh is observed inside the jet, carrying a fraction zhz_{h} of the jet longitudinal momentum (not labeled in the figure), a transverse momentum 𝒋⟂\bm{j}_{\perp} with azimuthal angle ϕ^h\hat{\phi}_{h}, and a transverse spin 𝑺h⊥\bm{S}_{h\bot} with azimuthal angle ϕ^Sh\hat{\phi}_{S_{h}}. Both 𝒋⟂\bm{j}_{\perp} and 𝑺h⊥\bm{S}_{h\bot} are measured with respect to the jet axis zJz_{J}, while both azimuthal angles ϕ^h\hat{\phi}_{h} and ϕ^Sh\hat{\phi}_{S_{h}} are measured within the jet transverse plane and with respect to xJx_{J}, the xx-axis that is rotated into jet coordinates33 3 Please see Eqs. 158 and 159 for the parameterization of 𝒋⟂\bm{j}_{\perp} and 𝑺h⊥\bm{S}_{h\bot}..

3.1 TMD FJFs in semi-inclusive jet productions

Again we start with the semi-inclusive TMD FJFs, which is an essential ingredient for studying the transverse momentum distribution of hadrons inside a jet in e.g., single inclusive jet production in proton-proton collisions (p+p→jet⁡(h)+Xp+p\to\mathrm{jet}(h)+X) or in electron-proton collisions (e+p→jet⁡(h)+Xe+p\to\mathrm{jet}(h)+X). Following the previous publication [34], we define the general correlators for TMD FJFs initiated by quark or gluon as:

Δh/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,Sh)\displaystyle\Delta^{h/q}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, S_h} =z2​Nc​δ​(zh−ωhωJ)​⟨0|δ​(ω−n¯⋅𝒫)​δ2​(𝒫⟂/zh+𝒋⟂)​χn​(0)|(J​h)​X⟩\displaystyle=\frac{z}{2N_{c}}\delta\pqty{z_h - \frac{\omega_h}{\omega_J}}\matrixelement{0}{\delta\pqty{\omega- \overline{n} \cdot\mathcal{P}} \delta^2 \pqty{\mathcal{P}_{\perp} / z_h+\boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}} \chi_n (0)}{(J h) X} (64)
×⟨(J​h)​X|χ¯n​(0)|0⟩,\displaystyle\quad\times\matrixelement{(J h) X}{\overline{\chi}_n(0)}{0},
Δh/g,μ​ν​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,Sh)\displaystyle\Delta^{h/g,\mu\nu}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, S_h} =z​ω(d−2)​(Nc2−1)​δ​(zh−ωhωJ)\displaystyle=\frac{z\omega}{(d-2)\pqty{N_c^2-1}}\delta\pqty{z_h-\frac{\omega_h}{\omega_J}} (65)
×⟨0|δ​(ω−n¯⋅𝒫)​δ2​(𝒫⟂/zh+𝒋⟂)​ℬn⟂μ​(0)|(J​h)​X⟩​⟨(J​h)​X|ℬn⟂ν​(0)|0⟩,\displaystyle\quad\times\matrixelement{0}{\delta\pqty{\omega- \overline{n} \cdot\mathcal{P}} \delta^2 \pqty{\mathcal{P}_{\perp} / z_h + \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}} \mathcal{B}_{n \perp}^{\mu}(0)}{(J h) X}\matrixelement{(J h) X}{\mathcal{B}_{n \perp}^{\nu} (0)}{0}\,,

where we have the energy fractions zz and zhz_{h} defined the same as in . One can parameterize these correlators at the leading power [40, 34]:

Δh/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,Sh)\displaystyle\Delta^{h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp},S_{h}) =Δh/q⁡[n̸]​n¯2−Δh/q⁡[n̸​γ5]​n¯​γ52+Δh/q⁡[i​nν​σk​ν​γ5]​i​n¯μ​σk​μ​γ52,\displaystyle=\Delta^{h/q\,[\not{n}]}\frac{\not{\overline{n}}}{2}-\Delta^{h/q\,[\not{n}\gamma_{5}]}\frac{\not{\overline{n}}\gamma_{5}}{2}+\Delta^{h/q\,[in_{\nu}\sigma^{k\nu}\gamma_{5}]}\frac{i\overline{n}_{\mu}\sigma^{k\mu}\gamma_{5}}{2}\,, (66)
Δh/g,k​l​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,Sh)\displaystyle\Delta^{h/g,kl}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp},S_{h}) =12​δTk​l​(δTm​n​Δh/g,m​n)−i2​ϵTk​l​(i​ϵTm​n​Δh/g,m​n)+S^​Δh/g,k​l.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{T}^{kl}\pqty{\delta_T^{mn} \Delta^{h/g, mn}}-\frac{i}{2}\epsilon_{T}^{kl}\pqty{i \epsilon_T^{mn} \Delta^{h/g, mn}}+\hat{S}\Delta^{h/g,kl}\,. (67)

Here we have defined Δh/q⁡[Γ]≡14​Tr⁡(Δh/q​Γ)\Delta^{h/q[\Gamma]}\equiv\frac{1}{4}\Tr(\Delta^{h/q} \Gamma), and we have S^​Ok​l=12​(Ok​l+Ol​k−δTk​l​Oρ​ρ)\hat{S}O^{kl}=\frac{1}{2}\pqty{O^{kl} + O^{lk} - \delta_T^{kl}O^{\rho\rho}} and δTk​l=−gTk​l\delta_{T}^{kl}=-g_{T}^{kl}. The three terms on the right-hand side of Eq. 66 correspond (in order) to the TMD FJFs with unpolarized, longitudinally polarized, and transversely polarized initial quarks. On the other hand, the three terms on the right-hand side of Eq. 67 correspond to unpolarized, circularly polarized, and linearly polarized gluons. More details have been presented in the previous work [34]. For completeness, here we provide the parameterization of quark TMD FJFs:

Δh/q⁡[n̸]\displaystyle\Delta^{h/q[\not{n}]} =𝒟1h/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−ϵTk​l​j⟂k​Sh⟂lzh​Mh​𝒟1​T⟂h/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{1}^{h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{\epsilon^{kl}_{T}j_{\perp}^{k}S_{h\perp}^{l}}{z_{h}M_{h}}\mathcal{D}_{1T}^{\perp h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})\,, (68)
Δh/q⁡[n̸​γ5]\displaystyle\Delta^{h/q[\not{n}\gamma_{5}]} =λh​𝒢1​Lh/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−𝒋⟂⋅𝑺h⟂zh​Mh​𝒢1​Th/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂),\displaystyle=\lambda_{h}\mathcal{G}_{1L}^{h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{\bm{j}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{S}_{h\perp}}{z_{h}M_{h}}\mathcal{G}_{1T}^{h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})\,, (69)
Δh/q⁡[i​nν​σk​ν​γ5]\displaystyle\Delta^{h/q[in_{\nu}\sigma^{k\nu}\gamma_{5}]} =Sh⟂k​ℋ1h/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−ϵTk​l​j⟂lzh​Mh​ℋ1⟂h/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−j⟂kzh​Mh​λh​ℋ1​L⟂h/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)\displaystyle=S_{h\perp}^{k}\mathcal{H}_{1}^{h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{\epsilon^{kl}_{T}j_{\perp}^{l}}{z_{h}M_{h}}\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\perp h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{j_{\perp}^{k}}{z_{h}M_{h}}\lambda_{h}{\mathcal{H}_{1L}^{\perp h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})}
+j⟂k​𝒋⟂⋅𝑺h⟂−12​𝒋⟂2​Sh⟂kzh2​Mh2​ℋ1​T⟂h/q​(z,zh,𝒋⟂),\displaystyle\quad+\frac{j_{\perp}^{k}\bm{j}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{S}_{h\perp}-\frac{1}{2}\bm{j}_{\perp}^{2}S_{h\perp}^{k}}{z_{h}^{2}M_{h}^{2}}\mathcal{H}_{1T}^{\perp h/q}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})\,, (70)

The functions 𝒟\mathcal{D}, 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H} on the right-hand side of Eqs. 68, 69 and 70 represent the TMD FJFs initiated by unpolarized, longitudinally polarized, and transversely polarized initial quark respectively. The parameterization for gluon TMD FJFs is given by

δTk​l​Δh/g,k​l\displaystyle\delta_{T}^{kl}\Delta^{h/g,kl} =𝒟1h/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−ϵTi​j​j⟂i​Sh⟂jzh​Mh​𝒟1⟂h/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{1}^{h/g}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{\epsilon^{ij}_{T}j_{\perp}^{i}S_{h\perp}^{j}}{z_{h}M_{h}}\mathcal{D}_{1}^{\perp h/g}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})\,, (71)
i​ϵTk​l​Δh/g,k​l\displaystyle i\epsilon_{T}^{kl}\Delta^{h/g,kl} =λh​𝒢1​Lh/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−𝒋⟂⋅𝑺h⟂zh​Mh​𝒢1​Th/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂),\displaystyle=\lambda_{h}\mathcal{G}_{1L}^{h/g}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{\bm{j}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{S}_{h\perp}}{z_{h}M_{h}}\mathcal{G}_{1T}^{h/g}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})\,, (72)
S^​Δh/g,k​l\displaystyle\hat{S}\Delta^{h/g,kl} =j⟂k​j⟂l2​zh2​Mh2​ℋ1⟂h/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−ϵTj⟂{kSh⟂l}+ϵTSh⟂{kj⟂l}8​zh​Mh​ℋ1​Th/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)\displaystyle=\frac{j_{\perp}^{k}j_{\perp}^{l}}{2z_{h}^{2}M_{h}^{2}}\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\perp h/g}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})-\frac{\epsilon_{T}^{j_{\perp}\{k}S_{h\perp}^{l\}}+\epsilon_{T}^{S_{h\perp}\{k}j_{\perp}^{l\}}}{8z_{h}M_{h}}\mathcal{H}_{1T}^{h/g}(z,z_{h},\bm{j}_{\perp})
+ϵTj⟂{kj⟂l}4​zh2​Mh2​(λh​ℋ1​L⟂,h/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)−𝒋⟂⋅𝑺h⟂zh​Mh​ℋ1​T⟂h/g​(z,zh,𝒋⟂)),\displaystyle\quad+\frac{\epsilon_{T}^{j_{\perp}\{k}j_{\perp}^{l\}}}{4z_{h}^{2}M_{h}^{2}}\pqty{ \lambda_h \mathcal{H}_{1L}^{\perp, h/g} (z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}) - \frac{\boldsymbol{j}_{\perp} \cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{h \perp}}{z_h M_h} \mathcal{H}_{1T}^{\perp h/g} (z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}) }\,, (73)

where the functions 𝒟\mathcal{D}, 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H} represent the TMD FJFs initiated by unpolarized, circularly polarized, and linearly polarized gluons, respectively. The two 𝒢\mathcal{G} functions with circularly polarized gluons are anti-symmetric of indices k,l=1,2k,\,l=1,2, and the four ℋ\mathcal{H} functions related to linearly polarized gluons are symmetric and traceless combinations of k,l=1,2k,\,l=1,2. We have adopted the notation vT{kwTl}=vTkwTl+vTlwTkv_{T}^{\{k}w_{T}^{l\}}=v_{T}^{k}w_{T}^{l}+v_{T}^{l}w_{T}^{k} as in [39, 13].

Since TMD FJFs represent the hadron fragmentation inside a fully reconstructed jet, their physical meaning is similar to that of standard TMD FFs as reviewed in [40]. Naturally, we adopt the calligraphic font of the letters used by the corresponding TMD FFs as the notations of TMD FJFs. For example, ℋ1h/q\mathcal{H}_{1}^{h/q} in Eq. 70 is the so-called quark transversity TMD FJFs, i.e., a transversely polarized quark initiates a jet, in which a transversely polarized hadron is observed. On the other hand, 𝒢1​Lh/g\mathcal{G}_{1L}^{h/g} in Eq. 72 is the helicity gluon TMD FJFs, i.e., a longitudinally polarized gluon initiates a jet, in which a longitudinally polarized hadron is observed.

In this study, we focus on the kinematic region ΛQCD≲j⟂≪pT​R\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}\lesssim j_{\perp}\ll p_{T}R, necessitating the adoption of the TMD factorization [20]. In the previous work [23], the TMD factorization for transverse momentum distribution of unpolarized hadrons inside the jet was derived. Over there, the evolution equations are based on the separate rapidity renormalization group equations for the so-called “unsubtracted” TMD FFs and soft functions. Below, in the process of reviewing the TMD factorization, we update the formalism with the more recent language outlined in the TMD Handbook [13]. This new formalism makes the evolution of the in-jet TMD FJFs simpler and more transparent than before. We then present the hard matching functions, where the expressions for longitudinally and transversely polarized cases are provided here for the first time.

3.1.1 TMD Factorization

In the kinematic region under consideration, the radiation relevant at leading power is restricted to collinear radiation within the jet, characterized by the momentum that scales as pc=[pc+,pc−,pc⟂]∼pc−​[λ2,1,λ]p_{c}=\bqty{p_c^+, p_c^-, p_{c\perp}}\sim p_{c}^{-}\bqty{\lambda^2, 1, \lambda}, where the power counting parameter λ∼j⟂/pT\lambda\sim j_{\perp}/p_{T}. Additionally, soft radiation of order j⟂j_{\perp} is also relevant. It is worth noting that harder emissions are only permitted outside the jet cone and will thus only impact the determination of the jet axis. Consequently, the hadron transverse momentum j⟂j_{\perp}, which is defined with respect to the jet axis, remains intact from the radiations external to the jet. Taking the unpolarized case as an example, a factorized formalism for the unpolarized TMD FJFs within SCET can be formulated [23]:

𝒟1h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1}^{h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iU​(z,pT​R,μ)​∫d2𝒌⟂​d2𝝀⟂​δ2​(zh​𝝀⟂+𝒌⟂−𝒋⟂)\displaystyle=\hat{H}^{U}_{c\to i}\pqty{z, p_T R, \mu}\int\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}}\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp}}\delta^{2}\pqty{z_h \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp} + \boldsymbol{k}_{\perp} - \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}}
×D1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒌⟂,μ,ζ/ν2)​Si​(𝝀⟂,μ,ν​ℛ/2),\displaystyle\quad\times D_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2}S_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2}\,, (74)

where Si​(𝝀⟂,μ,ν​ℛ/2)S_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2} is the in-jet soft function, and D1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒌⟂,μ,ζ/ν2)D_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2} is the “unsubtracted” TMD FFs with the superscript “(u)(u)” to emphasize this fact. Here μ\mu is the standard renormalization scale as above while ν\nu is a rapidity scale associated with the rapidity divergence [75, 76], and ζ\zeta is the so-called Collins-Soper scale [20]. We also have a scale ζJ\zeta_{J} to be defined below. The δ\delta function establishes a relationship between the hadron transverse momentum 𝒋⟂\bm{j}_{\perp}, relative to the jet axis, and two other momenta: the transverse momentum 𝝀⟂\bm{\lambda}_{\perp} of soft radiation, and the hadron transverse momentum 𝒌⟂\bm{k}_{\perp} with respect to the fragmenting parton. Notice that 𝝀⟂\bm{\lambda}_{\perp} is multiplied by zhz_{h} to adjust for the dissimilarity between the fragmenting parton and the observed hadron. The relationship among the three aforementioned transverse momenta is illustrated in Fig. 4.

As is common practice in TMD physics, we convert the aforementioned expression from the transverse momentum space to the coordinate bb-space with the following transformation:

𝒟1h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1}^{h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iU​(z,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle=\hat{H}^{U}_{c\to i}\pqty{z, p_T R, \mu} (75)
×∫d2𝒃(2​π)2​ei​𝒋⟂⋅𝒃/zh​D~1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζ/ν2)​S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2),\displaystyle\quad\times\int\frac{\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{b}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}e^{i\bm{j}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{b}/z_{h}}\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2}\widetilde{S}_{i}(\bm{b},\mu,\nu\mathcal{R}/2)\,,

where we have defined the D~1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζ/ν2)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2} and S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2)\widetilde{S}_{i}(\bm{b},\mu,\nu\mathcal{R}/2) in Fourier bb-space with i=q,gi=q,\,g as:

D~1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζ/ν2)\displaystyle\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2} =1zh2∫d2𝒌⟂e−i𝒌⟂⋅𝒃/zhD1h/i⁡(u)(zh,k⟂,μ,ζ/ν2)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{z_{h}^{2}}\int\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}}e^{-i\bm{k}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{b}/z_{h}}D_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, k_{\perp}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2}
=1zh2​∫dk⟂​k⟂​2​π​J0​(b​k⟂zh)​D1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,k⟂,μ,ζ/ν2),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{z_{h}^{2}}\int\differential{k_{\perp}}k_{\perp}2\pi J_{0}\pqty{\frac{b k_{\perp}}{z_h}}D_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, k_\perp, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2}\,, (76)
S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2)\displaystyle\widetilde{S}_{i}(\bm{b},\mu,\nu\mathcal{R}/2) =∫d2𝝀⟂e−i𝝀⟂⋅𝒃Si(𝝀⟂,μ,ν​ℛ/2),\displaystyle=\int\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{\lambda_{\perp}}}e^{-i\bm{\lambda}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{b}}S_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2}\,, (77)

where J0​(b​k⊥/zh)J_{0}\pqty{b k_{\bot} / z_h} is the Bessel function of the first kind. The μ\mu- and ν\nu-renormalization group equations for the “unsubstracted” TMD FFs D1h/i⁡(u)D_{1}^{h/i(u)} are well known:

μ​ddμ​ln⁡D~1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζ/ν2)\displaystyle\mu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\mu}}\ln\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2} =γμ,iD​(μ,ζ/ν2),\displaystyle=\gamma_{\mu,i}^{D}(\mu,\zeta/\nu^{2})\,, (78)
ν​ddν​ln⁡D~1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζ/ν2)\displaystyle\nu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\nu}}\ln\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2} =γν,iD​(b,μ),\displaystyle=\gamma_{\nu,i}^{D}(b,\mu)\,, (79)

where the leading order μ\mu- and ν\nu-anomalous dimensions are given by:

γμ,qD​(μ,ζ/ν2)\displaystyle\gamma_{\mu,q}^{D}(\mu,\zeta/\nu^{2}) =αsπ​CF​(ln⁡(ν2ζ)+32),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{F}\pqty{\ln(\frac{\nu^2}{\zeta}) + \frac{3}{2}}\,, (80)
γμ,gD​(μ,ζ/ν2)\displaystyle\gamma_{\mu,g}^{D}(\mu,\zeta/\nu^{2}) =αsπ​CA​(ln⁡(ν2ζ)+β02​CA),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{A}\pqty{\ln(\frac{\nu^2}{\zeta}) + \frac{\beta_0}{2C_A}}\,, (81)
γν,iD​(b,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{\nu,i}^{D}(b,\mu) =αsπ​Ci​ln⁡(μ2μb2),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{i}\ln(\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_b^2})\,, (82)

with Cq=CFC_{q}=C_{F}, Cg=CAC_{g}=C_{A}, and μb≡2​e−γE/b\mu_{b}\equiv 2e^{-\gamma_{E}}/b.

On the other hand, the in-jet soft function up to the NLO is given by [23, 77, 41]:

S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2)=1+αs2​π​Ci​[−12​ln2(μ2μb2)−ln⁡(μ2μb2)​ln⁡(ν2​tan2(ℛ/2)μ2)−π212].\widetilde{S}_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2}=1+\frac{\alpha_{s}}{2\pi}C_{i}\bqty{ - \frac{1}{2} \ln[2](\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_b^2}) - \ln(\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_b^2}) \ln(\frac{\nu^2 \tan[2](\mathcal{R}/2)}{\mu^2}) - \frac{\pi^2}{12} }\,. (83)

The corresponding μ\mu- and ν\nu-renormalization group equations are given by:

μ​ddμ​ln⁡S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2)\displaystyle\mu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\mu}}\ln\widetilde{S}_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2} =γμ,iS​(b,μ,ν​ℛ/2),\displaystyle=\gamma_{\mu,i}^{S}\pqty{b, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2}\,, (84)
ν​ddν​ln⁡S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2)\displaystyle\nu\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\nu}}\ln\widetilde{S}_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2} =γν,iS​(b,μ),\displaystyle=\gamma_{\nu,i}^{S}\pqty{b, \mu}\,, (85)

where the anomalous dimensions are given by:

γμ,iS​(b,μ,ν​ℛ/2)\displaystyle\gamma_{\mu,i}^{S}\pqty{b, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2} =−αsπ​Ci​ln⁡(ν2​tan2(ℛ/2)μ2),\displaystyle=-\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{i}\ln(\frac{\nu^2 \tan[2](\mathcal{R}/2)}{\mu^2})\,, (86)
γν,iS​(b,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{\nu,i}^{S}\pqty{b, \mu} =−αsπ​Ci​ln⁡(μ2μb2).\displaystyle=-\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{i}\ln(\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_b^2})\,. (87)

It is instructive to compare this in-jet soft function S~i\widetilde{S}_{i} with the standard soft function S~n​n¯,i​(𝒃,μ,ν)\widetilde{S}_{n\overline{n},i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu}, which arises in the TMD factorization for the semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS) and Drell-Yan production (involving quarks) or for the Higgs production in proton-proton collisions (involving gluons), whose expression is given by:

S~n​n¯,i​(𝒃,μ,ν)=1+αsπ​Ci​[−12​ln2(μ2μb2)−ln⁡(μ2μb2)​ln⁡(ν2μ2)−π212].\displaystyle\widetilde{S}_{n\overline{n},i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu}=1+\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{i}\bqty{ - \frac{1}{2} \ln[2](\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_b^2}) - \ln(\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_b^2}) \ln(\frac{\nu^2}{\mu^2}) - \frac{\pi^2}{12} }\,. (88)

After replacing ν→ν​tan⁡(ℛ/2)\nu\to\nu\tan(\mathcal{R}/2), the in-jet soft function S~i\widetilde{S}_{i} is exactly equal to S~n​n¯,i\sqrt{\widetilde{S}_{n\overline{n},i}} at the NLO:

S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2)=S~n​n¯,i​(𝒃,μ,ν)|ν→ν​tan⁡(ℛ/2).\displaystyle\widetilde{S}_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu\mathcal{R}/2}=\left.\sqrt{\widetilde{S}_{n\overline{n},i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \nu}}\right|_{\nu\to\nu\tan(\mathcal{R}/2)}\,. (89)

Now since the standard “subtracted” TMD FFs are defined as a combination of “unsubtracted” TMD FFs D~1h/i⁡(u)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)} and S~i\widetilde{S}_{i} [13], we would define the “subtracted” in-jet TMD FFs as a product of D~1h/i⁡(u)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)} and S~i\widetilde{S}_{i} as follows:

D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)≡D~1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζ/ν2)​S~i​(𝒃,μ,ν​ℛ/2),\displaystyle\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}\equiv\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta/\nu^2}\widetilde{S}_{i}(\bm{b},\mu,\nu\mathcal{R}/2)\,, (90)

where the rapidity divergences cancel out between D1h/i⁡(u)D_{1}^{h/i(u)} and S~i\widetilde{S}_{i} due to the sign difference shown in Eqs. 82 and 87. At the same time, we find that a slightly different Collins-Soper scale ζJ\zeta_{J} arises in the in-jet “subtracted” TMD FFs, which is related to the Collins-Soper scale ζ\zeta for the standard TMD FFs,

ζJ≡ζ​ℛ/2=pT​R,\displaystyle\sqrt{\zeta_{J}}\equiv\sqrt{\zeta}\,\mathcal{R}/2=p_{T}R\,, (91)

where we have used tan⁡(ℛ/2)≈ℛ/2\tan(\mathcal{R}/2)\approx\mathcal{R}/2 for narrow jets with ℛ≪1\mathcal{R}\ll 1. Note that in our regularization scheme, the natural Collins-Soper scale for TMD FFs is ζ=ωJ=2​EJ=2​pT​cosh⁡(η)\sqrt{\zeta}=\omega_{J}=2E_{J}=2p_{T}\cosh{\eta} and using ℛ=R/cosh⁡(η)\mathcal{R}=R/\cosh{\eta}, we obtain the natural scale ζJ\sqrt{\zeta_{J}} for the unpolarized TMD FJFs, which is simply pT​Rp_{T}R. With this newly defined Collins-Soper scale ζJ\zeta_{J}, following [13, 78], we can thus convert the ν\nu-RG equations above as:

ddln⁡(ζJ)​ln⁡(D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ))=K~​(b,μ),\displaystyle\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\ln{\sqrt{\zeta_J}}}}\ln{\widetilde{D}_1^{h/i} \pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}}=\widetilde{K}(b,\mu)\,, (92)

where K~​(b,μ)=−γν,iD​(b,μ)\widetilde{K}(b,\mu)=-\gamma_{\nu,i}^{D}(b,\mu) in Eq. 82 is the so-called Collins-Soper evolution kernel. In the small-bb region where 1/b≫ΛQCD1/b\gg\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}, it can be computed perturbatively and the four-loop expressions are available in [79, 80]. Notice that K~​(b,μ)\widetilde{K}(b,\mu) would become non-perturbative in the large-bb region, see recent numerical computations in lattice QCD [81, 82, 83, 84, 85]. On the other hand, the standard μ\mu-RG equation is given by:

ddln⁡(μ)​ln⁡(D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ))=γμi​[αs​(μ),ζJ/μ2],\displaystyle\frac{\differential{}}{\differential{\ln{\mu}}}\ln{\widetilde{D}_1^{h/i} \pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}}=\gamma_{\mu}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s(\mu), \zeta_J/\mu^2}\,, (93)

where the anomalous dimension γμi​[αs​(μ),ζJ/μ2]\gamma_{\mu}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s(\mu), \zeta_J/\mu^2} are given by:

γμi​[αs​(μ),ζJ/μ2]=−Γcuspi​[αs​(μ)]​ln⁡(ζJμ2)+γμi​[αs​(μ)],\displaystyle\gamma_{\mu}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s(\mu), \zeta_J/\mu^2}=-\Gamma_{\mathrm{cusp}}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s(\mu)}\,\ln(\frac{\zeta_J}{\mu^2})+\gamma_{\mu}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s(\mu)}\,, (94)

where we have written the more general form [13] with Γcuspi\Gamma_{\mathrm{cusp}}^{i} and γμi\gamma_{\mu}^{i} the cusp and non-cusp anomalous dimensions. They are perturbatively expanded as Γcuspi​[αs]=∑n=1Γn−1i​(αs4​π)n\Gamma_{\mathrm{cusp}}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s}=\sum_{n=1}\Gamma_{n-1}^{i}\pqty{\frac{\alpha_s}{4\pi}}^{n} and γμi​[αs]=∑n=1γni​(αs4​π)n\gamma_{\mu}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s}=\sum_{n=1}\gamma_{n}^{i}\pqty{\frac{\alpha_s}{4\pi}}^{n} and at the next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) order, they are given by [86, 31]:

Γ0q\displaystyle\Gamma_{0}^{q} =4​CF,Γ1q=4​CF​[(679−π23)​CA−209​TF​nf],γ0q=6​CF,\displaystyle=4C_{F}\,,\qquad\Gamma_{1}^{q}=4C_{F}\bqty{\pqty{\frac{67}{9}-\frac{\pi^2}{3}} C_A - \frac{20}{9} T_F n_f}\,,\qquad\gamma_{0}^{q}=6C_{F}\,, (95)
Γ0,1g\displaystyle\Gamma_{0,1}^{g} =CACF​Γ0,1q,γ0g=2​β0.\displaystyle=\frac{C_{A}}{C_{F}}\Gamma_{0,1}^{q}\,,\qquad\gamma_{0}^{g}=2\beta_{0}\,. (96)

One can solve the ζJ\zeta_{J}- and μ\mu-RG evolution equation to obtain the “subtracted” in-jet TMD FFs:

D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)=D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ0,ζ0)\displaystyle\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}=\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu_0, \zeta_0} exp⁡[∫μ0μdμ′μ′​γμi​[αs​(μ),ζJ/μ2]]\displaystyle\exp[\int_{\mu_{0}}^{\mu}\frac{\differential{\mu'}}{\mu^{\prime}}\gamma_{\mu}^{i}\bqty{\alpha_s(\mu), \zeta_J/\mu^2}]
×\displaystyle\times exp⁡[K~​(b,μ0)​ln⁡(ζJζ0)].\displaystyle\exp[\widetilde{K}(b,\mu_{0})\ln(\frac{\sqrt{\zeta_J}}{\sqrt{\zeta_0}})]\,. (97)

One typically evolves the in-jet TMD FFs D~1h/i\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i} from the initial scale μ0=ζ0=μb\mu_{0}=\sqrt{\zeta_{0}}=\mu_{b} to the final scale μ∼pT\mu\sim p_{T} of the jet and ζJ=pT​R\sqrt{\zeta_{J}}=p_{T}R as mentioned above. On the other hand, at the initial scale μ0=ζ0=μb\mu_{0}=\sqrt{\zeta_{0}}=\mu_{b}, one can expand D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ0,ζ0)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu_0, \zeta_0} in terms of the corresponding collinear FFs when μb≫ΛQCD\mu_{b}\gg\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}.

To generalize the above TMD factorization to the polarized TMD FJFs, let us define the following operator 𝒞\mathscr{C}:

𝒞⁡[D~h/i,(n)]≡∫bn+1​db2​π​n!​(zh2​Mh2j⟂)n​Jn​(j⟂​bzh)​D~h/i,(n)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ),\displaystyle\mathscr{C}[\widetilde{D}^{h/i,(n)}]\equiv\int\frac{b^{n+1}\differential{b}}{2\pi n!}\pqty{\frac{z_h^2 M_h^2}{j_{\perp}}}^{n}J_{n}\pqty{\frac{j_{\perp} b}{z_h}}\widetilde{D}^{h/i,(n)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}\,, (98)

where D~h/i,(n)\widetilde{D}^{h/i,(n)} is nn-th moment of the TMD FFs in the Fourier bb-space:

D~h/i,(n)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)=1zh2​2​π​n!(zh2​Mh2)n​∫dk⟂​k⟂​(k⟂b)n​Jn​(b​k⟂zh)​Dh/i​(zh,𝒌⟂,μ,ζJ).\widetilde{D}^{h/i,(n)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}=\frac{1}{z_{h}^{2}}\frac{2\pi n!}{\pqty{z_h^2 M_h^2}^{n}}\int\differential{k_{\perp}}k_{\perp}\pqty{\frac{k_{\perp}}{b}}^{n}J_{n}\pqty{\frac{b k_{\perp}}{z_h}}D^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}, \mu, \zeta_J}\,. (99)

In addition, we suppress the superscript (0)(0) when n=0n=0. One can easily verify that with n=0n=0 and D=D1D=D_{1}, the combination of Eqs. 76 and 90 would lead to Eq. 99. It is important to realize that each in-jet TMD FF D~h/i,(n)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)\widetilde{D}^{h/i,(n)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J} would follow the same Collins-Soper evolution equation as in Eq. 92, as well as the same μ\mu-RG equation as in Eq. 93. They are identical to the standard TMD FFs with the replacement ζ\zeta by ζJ\zeta_{J}. Thus, their evolved results would be given exactly by Eq. 97, except one replaces D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J} by the corresponding TMD FFs D~h/i,(n)​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)\widetilde{D}^{h/i,(n)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J} defined above and given below for specific TMD FFs. Note that the evolved in-jet unpolarized TMD FFs D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J} is given by Eq. 97, which depends on the TMD FFs D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ0,ζ0)\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu_0, \zeta_0} at the initial scale μ0\mu_{0} and ζ0\zeta_{0}. Often, one further matches the TMD FFs at the initial scales onto collinear FFs. For example, the matching coefficients for the unpolarized TMD FFs are known up to N3​LO{\mathrm{N}^{3}\mathrm{LO}} [87, 88]. On the other hand, the matching coefficients for H~1h/q\widetilde{H}_{1}^{h/q} are known up to NNLO [89]. We can now write down the factorization for all the TMD FJFs as:

𝒟1h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1}^{h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iU​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[D~1h/i],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{U}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}}\,, (100)
𝒟1​T⟂,h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1T}^{\perp,h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iU​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[D~1​T⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{U}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{D}_{1T}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (101)
𝒢1​Lh/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{1L}^{h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iL​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[G~1​Lh/i],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{L}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{G}_{1L}^{h/i}}\,, (102)
𝒢1​Th/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{1T}^{h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iL​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[G~1​Th/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{L}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{G}_{1T}^{h/i, (1)}}\,, (103)
ℋ1h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{1}^{h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iT​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[H~1h/i],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{T}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1}^{h/i}}\,, (104)
ℋ1⟂,h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\perp,h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iT​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[H~1⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{T}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (105)
ℋ1​L⟂,h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{1L}^{\perp,h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iT​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[H~1​L⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{T}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1L}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (106)
ℋ1​T⟂,h/c​(z,zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{1T}^{\perp,h/c}\pqty{z, z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_TR, \mu, \zeta_J} =H^c→iT​(z,pT​R,μ)​𝒞​[H~1​T⟂,h/i,(2)].\displaystyle=\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{T}(z,p_{T}R,\mu)\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1T}^{\perp, h/i, (2)}}\,. (107)

Here the superscripts UU, LL and TT of H^c→i\hat{H}_{c\to i} represent unpolarized, longitudinally polarized and transversely polarized hard matching functions, respectively. The hard matching functions will be provided in the next subsection. The above equations also show how various TMD FJFs are matched onto their corresponding TMD FFs, with which the matching of the scenarios listed in Table 1 can be performed.

3.1.2 Hard matching functions

The hard matching functions H^c→iU,L,T\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{U,L,T} describe the out-of-jet radiation during which an energetic parton cc, generated in a hard scattering event, undergoes a splitting into a parton ii, which subsequently initiates a jet with energy ωJ\omega_{J} and radius RR. The hard matching functions for the unpolarized case H^c→iU\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{U} are available previously [21, 59, 65, 90]. They describe the splitting from an unpolarized initial parton cc to an unpolarized parton ii, irrespective of the polarization of the final-state hadron inside the jet. Because of that, we would have the same hard matching functions for both unpolarized TMD FJFs 𝒟1h/c\mathcal{D}_{1}^{h/c} and the polarized TMD FJFs 𝒟1​T⟂,h/c\mathcal{D}_{1T}^{\perp,h/c}, as indicated in Eqs. 100 and 101. We remind the reader that 𝒟1​T⟂,h/c\mathcal{D}_{1T}^{\perp,h/c} stands for the situation where an unpolarized parton cc splits into an unpolarized parton ii that fragments into a transversely polarized hadron hh. This arises from the correlation between the hadron’s transverse momentum with respect to the jet axis and the transverse spin of the hadron itself. For the same reasons, we have the same longitudinally polarized hard matching functions H^c→iL\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{L} for the TMD FJFs 𝒢1​Lh/c\mathcal{G}_{1L}^{h/c} and 𝒢1​Th/c\mathcal{G}_{1T}^{h/c}, as indicated in Eqs. 102 and 103. Likewise, we have the same transversely polarized hard matching functions H^c→iT\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{T} for the TMD FJFs ℋ1h/c\mathcal{H}_{1}^{h/c}, ℋ1⟂,h/c\mathcal{H}_{1}^{\perp,h/c}, ℋ1​L⟂,h/c\mathcal{H}_{1L}^{\perp,h/c}, and ℋ1​T⟂,h/c\mathcal{H}_{1T}^{\perp,h/c}, as indicated in Eqs. 104, 105, 106 and 107. Looking at Table 1, the FJFs listed in the same column possess identical hard matching functions, due to the fact that the parton polarization is the same in the same column.

For completeness, we list the unpolarized results H^c→iU\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{U} here. We then provide in addition the results H^c→iL,T\hat{H}_{c\to i}^{L,T} for the polarized cases.

where indices ii, jj and kk all represent partons qq or gg. For the unpolarized hard matching functions, their anomalous dimensions γi​jU​(z,pT​R,μ)\gamma_{ij}^{U}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} are given by:

γq​qL​(z,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{qq}^{L}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} =αsπ​(Δ​Pq​q​(z)−CF​L​δ​(1−z)−3​CF2​δ​(1−z)),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}\pqty{\Delta P_{qq} \pqty{z} - C_F L \delta\pqty{1 - z} - \frac{3 C_F}{2} \delta\pqty{1 - z}}\,, (134)
γq​gL​(z,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{qg}^{L}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} =αsπ​Δ​Pg​q​(z),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}\Delta P_{gq}\pqty{z}\,, (135)
γg​gL​(z,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{gg}^{L}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} =αsπ​(Δ​Pg​g​(z)−CA​L​δ​(1−z)−β02​δ​(1−z)),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}\pqty{\Delta P_{g g} \pqty{z} - C_A L \delta\pqty{1 - z} - \frac{\beta_0}{2} \delta\pqty{1 - z}}\,, (136)
γg​qL​(z,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{gq}^{L}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} =αsπ​Δ​Pq​g​(z),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}\Delta P_{qg}\pqty{z}\,, (137)
γq​qT​(z,pT​R,μ)\displaystyle\gamma_{qq}^{T}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} =αsπ​(ΔT​Pq​q​(z)−CF​L​δ​(1−z)−3​CF2​δ​(1−z)).\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}\pqty{\Delta_T P_{q q} \pqty{z} - C_F L \delta\pqty{1 - z} - \frac{3 C_F}{2} \delta\pqty{1 - z}}\,. (138)

Obviously, the natural scale for the hard matching functions is μ∼pT​R\mu\sim p_{T}R as indicated in the logarithm LL in the perturbative results. Therefore, we can resum the large logarithms of jet radius ln⁡R\ln R by evolving the hard matching functions from scale μ∼pT​R\mu\sim p_{T}R to the hard scattering scale μ∼pT\mu\sim p_{T} with the RG equations. We notice that similar to the unpolarized case studied in [23]:

γi​jU​(z,pT​R,μ)=δi​j​δ​(1−z)​Γi​(pT​R,μ)+αsπ​Pj​i​(z),\gamma_{ij}^{U}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu}=\delta_{ij}\delta(1-z)\Gamma_{i}\pqty{p_TR, \mu}+\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}P_{ji}(z)\,, (139)

where Γi\Gamma_{i} are given by:

Γq​(pT​R,μ)=αsπ​CF​(−L−32),Γg​(pT​R,μ)=αsπ​CA​(−L−β02​CA).\Gamma_{q}\pqty{p_TR, \mu}=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{F}\pqty{- L - \frac{3}{2}}\,,\quad\Gamma_{g}\pqty{p_TR, \mu}=\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}C_{A}\pqty{- L - \frac{\beta_0}{2 C_A}}\,. (140)

Following the same exercise, we can express the anomalous dimensions γi​jL⁡(T)​(z,pT​R,μ)\gamma_{ij}^{L(T)}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu} in Eqs. 134, 135, 136, 137 and 138 into a general form:

γi​jL⁡(T)​(z,pT​R,μ)=δi​j​δ​(1−z)​Γi​(pT​R,μ)+αsπ​Δ(T)​Pj​i​(z),\gamma_{ij}^{L(T)}\pqty{z, p_TR, \mu}=\delta_{ij}\delta(1-z)\Gamma_{i}\pqty{p_TR, \mu}+\frac{\alpha_{s}}{\pi}\Delta_{(T)}P_{ji}(z)\,, (141)

where the functions Γi​(pT​R,μ)\Gamma_{i}\pqty{p_TR, \mu} in the first term are independent of polarization and are therefore the same as the unpolarized Γi\Gamma_{i} in Eq. 140.

3.2 TMD FJFs in exclusive jet production

For the exclusive jet production, exclusive TMD FJFs 𝒟~1h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\widetilde{\mathscr{D}}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} arises in the factorization formalism. Since one cannot have out-of-jet hard radiation as explained in Section 2.2, the factorization formalism in the j⟂≪pT​Rj_{\perp}\ll p_{T}R region would be given by

𝒟~1h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{D}}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =∫d2𝒌⟂​d2𝝀⟂​δ2​(zh​𝝀⟂+𝒌⟂−𝒋⟂)​D1h/i⁡(u)​(zh,𝒌⟂,μ,ζν2)​Si​(𝝀⟂,μ,ν​ℛ2)\displaystyle=\int\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}}\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp}}\delta^{2}\pqty{z_h \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp} + \boldsymbol{k}_{\perp} - \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}}D_{1}^{h/i(u)}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{k}_{\perp}, \mu, \frac{\zeta}{\nu^2}}S_{i}\pqty{\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\perp}, \mu, \frac{\nu\mathcal{R}}{2}}
=∫d2𝒃(2​π)2​ei​𝒋⟂⋅𝒃/zh​D~1h/i​(zh,𝒃,μ,ζJ),\displaystyle=\int\frac{\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{b}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}e^{i\bm{j}_{\perp}\cdot\bm{b}/z_{h}}\widetilde{D}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{b}, \mu, \zeta_J}\,, (142)

where we have used Eq. 90. Again for exclusive jet production, we no longer have the dependence on zz as in the semi-inclusive TMD FJFs. Following the same procedure as before, we can generalize this to the polarized exclusive TMD FJFs. With the operator 𝒞\mathscr{C} defined in Eq. 98, the unpolarized exclusive TMD FJFs are given by:

𝒟~1h/i​(zh,pT​R,𝒋⟂,μ,ζJ)=𝒞​[D~1h/i],\widetilde{\mathscr{D}}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, p_T {R}, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, \mu, \zeta_J}=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{D}_1^{h/i}}\,, (143)

Similarly for exclusive TMD FJFs with different polarizations, we have:

𝒟~1​T⟂,h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{D}}_{1T}^{\perp,h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[D~1​T⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{D}_{1T}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (144)
𝒢~1​Lh/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{G}}_{1L}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[G~1​Lh/i],\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{G}_{1L}^{h/i}}\,, (145)
𝒢~1​T⟂,h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{G}}_{1T}^{\perp,h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[G~1​T⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{G}_{1T}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (146)
ℋ~1h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{H}}_{1}^{h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[H~1h/i],\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1}^{h/i}}\,, (147)
ℋ~1⟂,h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{H}}_{1}^{\perp,h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[H~1⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (148)
ℋ~1​L⟂,h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{H}}_{1L}^{\perp,h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[H~1​L⟂,h/i,(1)],\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1L}^{\perp, h/i, (1)}}\,, (149)
ℋ~1​T⟂,h/i​(zh,𝒋⟂,pT​R,μ,ζJ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathscr{H}}_{1T}^{\perp,h/i}\pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, p_T R, \mu, \zeta_J} =𝒞​[H~1​T⟂,h/i,(2)].\displaystyle=\mathscr{C}\bqty{\widetilde{H}_{1T}^{\perp, h/i, (2)}}\,. (150)

4 Phenomenology

There has been growing phenomenological work for studying hadron distribution inside the jet, in particular in connection with the 3D imaging of the hadrons. For example, for single inclusive jet production in proton-proton collisions as well as electron-proton scatterings, unpolarized and polarized collinear hadron distribution inside the jet have been studied [25, 21, 34, 43]. The TMD distribution of hadrons inside the jet produced in transversely polarized proton-proton collisions is sensitive to the Collins TMD FFs and has been studied in [91]. For exclusive jet production, such as back-to-back ZZ+jet production in proton-proton collisions and back-to-back lepton+jet production in DIS, TMD hadron distribution inside jets has been studied [27, 42, 41, 92, 93].

Before we present the phenomenology, we first provide more details on TMD FFs. In previous sections, we have discussed the evolution of FJFs in the perturbative region, i.e., 1/b≫ΛQCD1/b\gg\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}. However, to do calculations for phenomenology, we must take care of the non-perturbative evolution of TMDs at the large-bb region. In order to do this, we adopt the b∗b_{*}-prescription [94]. Alternative approaches can be found in [95, 96, 97, 98, 99]. The b∗b_{*} is defined as:

b∗≡b1+b2/bmax2,b_{*}\equiv\frac{b}{\sqrt{1+b^{2}/b_{\max}^{2}}}\,, (151)

where we choose bmax=1.5​GeV−1b_{\max}=1.5~\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}. With this definition, the magnitude of b∗b_{*} approaches bb when b≪bmaxb\ll b_{\max}, and approaches bmaxb_{\max} in the large-bb region. For the perturbative contribution, we work at the NLL order, where we keep Γ0,1i\Gamma_{0,1}^{i} and γ0i\gamma_{0}^{i} in Eqs. 97 and 94. For the non-perturbative contribution, we include the following non-perturbative Sudakov factor [100, 101]:

SNPq​(b,Q0,ζJ)=g22​ln⁡(bb∗)​ln⁡(ζJQ0)+ghzh2​b2,S_{\mathrm{NP}}^{q}(b,Q_{0},\sqrt{\zeta_{J}})=\frac{g_{2}}{2}\ln(\frac{b}{b_*})\ln(\frac{\sqrt{\zeta_J}}{Q_0})+\frac{g_{h}}{z_{h}^{2}}b^{2}\,, (152)

where Q02=2.4​GeV2Q_{0}^{2}=2.4~\mathrm{GeV}^{2}, g2=0.84g_{2}=0.84 and gh=0.042g_{h}=0.042, and ζJ=pT​R\sqrt{\zeta_{J}}=p_{T}R following Eq. 91. For gluon TMD FFs, we use [23]:

SNPg​(b,Q0,ζJ)=CACF​g22​ln⁡(bb∗)​ln⁡(ζJQ0)+ghzh2​b2.S_{\mathrm{NP}}^{g}(b,Q_{0},\sqrt{\zeta_{J}})=\frac{C_{A}}{C_{F}}\frac{g_{2}}{2}\ln(\frac{b}{b_*})\ln(\frac{\sqrt{\zeta_J}}{Q_0})+\frac{g_{h}}{z_{h}^{2}}b^{2}\,. (153)

Now that we have properly addressed the non-perturbative evolution, we can proceed with predicting relevant observables. In this section, we provide two additional phenomenological examples. For the case of single inclusive jet production, we compute the transverse momentum distribution for hadrons inside the jet at RHIC kinematics, where a transversely polarized proton collides with an unpolarized proton, producing a jet with a transversely polarized Λ\Lambda-baryon inside. This process will be sensitive to both transversity distributions h1h_{1} and transversity TMD FJFs ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. For the exclusive jet production, we study back-to-back lepton jet production in lepton-proton collisions, where the incoming proton is transversely polarized and the final hadron inside the jet is longitudinally polarized. This observable is sensitive to the “worm-gear” TMD PDFs g1​Tg_{1T} and longitudinally polarized TMD FJFs 𝒢1​L\mathcal{G}_{1L}.

4.1 Transverse spin transfer to Λ\Lambda in jet in polarized p​ppp collisions

For semi-inclusive process, we consider the p​ppp collision in its center-of-mass frame:

p​(PA,SA)+p​(PB)→[jet⁡(pJ)​h​(zh,𝒋⟂,Sh)]+X,p\pqty{P_A, S_A}+p\pqty{P_B}\to\bqty{\mathrm{jet}(p_J) h \pqty{z_h, \boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}, S_h}}+X\,, (154)

where PAP_{A} and PBP_{B} are the momenta of the incident protons, SAS_{A} is the polarization of the proton AA. They are defined as:

PA\displaystyle P_{A} =s2​(1,0,0,1),PB=s2​(1,0,0,−1),\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}\pqty{1, 0, 0, 1},\quad P_{B}=\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}\pqty{1, 0, 0, -1}\,, (155)
SA\displaystyle S_{A} =[−λA​MApA−,λA​pA−MA,𝑺T],\displaystyle=\bqty{-\lambda_A \frac{M_A}{p_A^-}, \lambda_A \frac{p_A^-}{M_A}, \boldsymbol{S}_T}\,, (156)

where ss is the squared proton center of mass energy. Notice that SAS_{A} is written in light-cone coordinate defined in Eq. 3, and λA\lambda_{A} is the helicity of the incoming proton with mass MAM_{A}, pA−p_{A}^{-} is the large light-cone momentum of the proton AA, ϕS\phi_{S} is the azimuthal angle between the transverse spin 𝑺T\bm{S}_{T} of the initial proton and the reaction plane, with the reaction plane defined by the incoming beam direction and jet axis direction (painted yellow in Fig. 5). For the jet production, pJp_{J} is the jet momentum, with pTp_{T} being the magnitude of its transverse component:

pJ=(pT​cosh⁡(η),pT,0,pT​sinh⁡(η)).p_{J}=\pqty{p_T \cosh{\eta}, p_T, 0, p_T \sinh{\eta}}\,. (157)

Note here the yy-component of pJp_{J} is zero because we put the jet within the reaction plane (x​zxz-plane). The hadron inside the jet has a transverse momentum 𝒋⟂\bm{j}_{\perp} with respect to the jet axis, and collinear momentum fraction zhz_{h} of the jet momentum. Together with the hadron’s transverse spin 𝑺h⊥\bm{S}_{h\bot}, they are given by:

𝒋⟂\displaystyle\bm{j}_{\perp} =|𝒋⟂|​(cos⁡(ϕ^h)​cos⁡(θJ),sin⁡(ϕ^h),−cos⁡(ϕ^h)​sin⁡(θJ)),\displaystyle=\absolutevalue{\boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}}\pqty{\cos{\hat{\phi}_h} \cos{\theta_J}, \sin{\hat{\phi}_h}, -\cos{\hat{\phi}_h} \sin{\theta_J}}\,, (158)
𝑺h⊥\displaystyle\bm{S}_{h\bot} =|𝑺h⊥|​(cos⁡(ϕ^Sh)​cos⁡(θJ),sin⁡(ϕ^Sh),−cos⁡(ϕ^Sh)​sin⁡(θJ)),\displaystyle=\absolutevalue{\boldsymbol{S}_{h \bot}}\pqty{\cos{\hat{\phi}_{S_h}} \cos{\theta_J}, \sin{\hat{\phi}_{S_h}}, -\cos{\hat{\phi}_{S_h}} \sin{\theta_J}}\,, (159)

where θJ\theta_{J} is the angle between jet axis and zz-axis, ϕ^h\hat{\phi}_{h} is the azimuthal angle between the momentum php_{h} of the produced hadron and the reaction plane, and ϕ^Sh\hat{\phi}_{S_{h}} is the azimuthal angle between the transverse spin 𝑺h⊥\bm{S}_{h\bot} and the reaction plane. The “hat” that decorates ϕ^h\hat{\phi}_{h} and ϕ^Sh\hat{\phi}_{S_{h}} indicates that these angles are measured in the jet coordinates.

For single inclusive jet production, the most general azimuthal dependence44 4 Here we consider the situation where only one of the incoming hadrons could be polarized and the final-state hadron can be polarized. for the hadron zhz_{h} and 𝒋⟂\bm{j}_{\perp} distributions inside the jet is given by [34]:

dσp​(SA)+p→jet​h​(Sh)+Xdη​d2𝒑T​dzh​d2𝒋⟂\displaystyle\frac{\differential{\sigma^{p \pqty{S_A} + p \to\mathrm{jet} h \pqty{S_h} + X}}}{\differential{\eta}\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{p}_T}\differential{z_h}\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{j}_{\perp}}} =FU​U,U+|𝑺T|​sin⁡(ϕS−ϕ^h)​FT​U,Usin⁡(ϕS−ϕ^h)\displaystyle=F_{UU,U}+\absolutevalue{\boldsymbol{S}_T}\sin(\phi_{S} - \hat{\phi}_h)F^{\sin(\phi_{S} - \hat{\phi}_h)}_{TU,U}

where FA​B,CF_{AB,C} denotes the spin-dependent structure functions, with AA, BB and CC indicating the polarization of incoming proton AA, incoming proton BB (or electron), and the fragmented hadron inside the jet. λA\lambda_{A} and |𝑺⟂|\absolutevalue{\boldsymbol{S}_{\perp}} are the longitudinal and transverse spin of the initial polarized proton AA, while λh\lambda_{h} and |𝑺hT|\absolutevalue{\boldsymbol{S}_{h_T}} are the longitudinal and transverse polarization of the hadron inside jet measured in the fragmenting parton helicity frame.

where f1a/A​(x1,μ)f_{1}^{a/A}(x_{1},\mu) and f2b/B​(x2,μ)f_{2}^{b/B}(x_{2},\mu) are the collinear unpolarized PDFs in the proton with corresponding momentum fractions x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}, and σ^a​bc\hat{\sigma}_{ab}^{c} is the hard function for unpolarized parton aa, bb to unpolarized parton cc. s^=x1​x2​s,p^T=pT/z,η^=η−12​ln⁡(x1x2).\hat{s}=x_{1}x_{2}s\,,\quad\hat{p}_{T}=p_{T}/z\,,\quad\hat{\eta}=\eta-\frac{1}{2}\ln(\frac{x_1}{x_2})\,. (162)
